title: Logging and Diagnostic Output
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of logging and diagnostic output in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply logging and diagnostic output in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to avoiding sensitive data in logs and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Logging and Diagnostic Output through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding logging and diagnostic output helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Logging and Diagnostic Output helps you reason about using ruby's logger. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Using Ruby's Logger. Then connect it to Log levels and structured context. The remaining syllabus points—Avoiding sensitive data in logs—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

items.title: Assuming the happy path is enough
items.text: Test an empty value, a boundary value, and one invalid value before depending on the behavior.

items.title: Treating an example as a universal rule
items.text: Check Ruby version, runtime implementation, and third-party library documentation when behavior is version-sensitive.

items.title: Mixing too many concerns
items.text: Separate input parsing, domain behavior, and output so each piece is easier to test.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports logging and diagnostic output. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for logging and diagnostic output using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Avoiding sensitive data in logs), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. If the command fails, confirm `ruby --version`, inspect the full error message, and verify that required standard-library or gem dependencies are installed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain logging and diagnostic output, identify its place in exceptions, debugging, and diagnostics, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
